claim: From 26 April 2020 to 13 March 2021, 440,479 participants from 217,887 households in the COVID-19 Infection Survey had one or more RT-PCR results from nose and throat swabs.
source: From 26 April 2020 to 13 March 2021, 440,479 participants from 217,887 households in the COVID-19 Infection Survey had one or more RT-PCR results from nose and throat swabs (median eight results per participant [IQR 6–9, range 1–19]).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific numbers of participants and households with RT-PCR results during the specified time period.

claim: Of 3,312,159 RT-PCR test results, 27,902 (0.84%, 95% CI 0.83–0.85%) were positive.
source: Of 3,312,159 RT-PCR test results, 27,902 (0.84%, 95% CI 0.83–0.85%) were positive, in 21,831 individuals from 16,214 households.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific counts and percentages of positive RT-PCR test results from the study data.

claim: 10,317 (37%) swabs were positive for three genes, 11,012 (40%) for two genes, and 6,550 (23%) for one gene.
source: Overall, 10,317 (37%), 11,012 (40%), and 6550 (23%) swabs were positive for three, two, or one of the three SARS-CoV-2 genes (N protein, S protein, and ORF1ab), respectively (Table 1; 23 positives with missing Ct and gene detection excluded from this and all subsequent analysis; samples with only the S-gene detected generally not called positive, see Materials and methods).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific counts and percentages of swabs positive for different numbers of genes.

claim: The majority of two-gene positives (9513 [86%]) were ORF1ab+N positive from 16 November 2020 onwards, reflecting the emergence and expansion of B.1.1.7 (WHO Alpha) in the UK.
source: The majority of two-gene positives (9513 [86%]) were ORF1ab+N positive from 16 November 2020 onwards, reflecting the emergence and expansion of B.1.1.7 (WHO Alpha) in the UK (Walker et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific data on two-gene positives and cites a reference for the emergence of B.1.1.7.

claim: B.1.1.7 leads to S-gene target failure (SGTF) and was estimated to account for 88% of SGTF from 16 November 2020.
source: B.1.1.7 leads to S-gene target failure (SGTF) and was estimated to account for 88% of SGTF from this time (Public Health England, 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites Public Health England data for the estimate of B.1.1.7 accounting for SGTF.

claim: The overall median Ct was 29.2 (IQR 21.9–32.8; range 9.2–38.7), corresponding to a median viral load of ~215 copies/ml (IQR 14–56,400).
source: Taking the per-swab mean Ct across positive genes, the overall median Ct was 29.2 (IQR 21.9–32.8; range 9.2–38.7), reflecting the study's surveillance design testing individuals in the community at fixed timepoints regardless of symptoms. Based on calibration data (Appendix 1—figure 1), this corresponds to a median viral load of ~215 copies/ml (IQR 14–56,400).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific Ct values from the study data and references calibration data in a figure.

claim: Ct varied strongly by number of genes detected (Kruskal–Wallis p=0.0001), but not by their specific pattern after adjusting for number (p=0.08).
source: Ct varied strongly by number of genes detected (Kruskal–Wallis p=0.0001), but not by their specific pattern after adjusting for number (p=0.08).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results showing the relationship between Ct values and number of genes detected.

claim: Only 38 (0.1%) Ct values > 37 were recorded.
source: There is no fixed Ct threshold for determining positivity (see Materials and methods); however, only 38 (0.1%) Ct values > 37 were recorded (five positive on ORF1ab+N).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific counts of Ct values above 37.

claim: Single-gene positives almost invariably had Ct>30.
source: Of note, whilst single-gene positives almost invariably had Ct>30, with or without reported symptoms, triple-gene positives without reported symptoms had widely varying Ct, as did ORF1ab+N positives after 16 November 2020 (SGTF, compatible with B.1.1.7) (Figure 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes the pattern of Ct values in single-gene positives and references Figure 1.

claim: Triple-gene positives without reported symptoms had widely varying Ct.
source: Of note, whilst single-gene positives almost invariably had Ct>30, with or without reported symptoms, triple-gene positives without reported symptoms had widely varying Ct, as did ORF1ab+N positives after 16 November 2020 (SGTF, compatible with B.1.1.7) (Figure 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes the pattern of Ct values in triple-gene positives and references Figure 1.

claim: The percentage reporting symptoms increased linearly as Ct values dropped from 35 (~30% reporting symptoms around the positive test) to 28 (~60% reporting symptoms).
source: Furthermore, whilst the percentage reporting symptoms increased linearly as Ct values dropped from 35 (~30% reporting symptoms around the positive test) to 28 (~60% reporting symptoms), below 28 the percentages reporting symptoms increased only slightly (to ~70% at Ct=10) (Figure 2).
evidence: The manuscript describes the relationship between Ct values and symptom reporting and references Figure 2.

claim: Below Ct=28, the percentages reporting symptoms increased only slightly (to ~70% at Ct=10).
source: Furthermore, whilst the percentage reporting symptoms increased linearly as Ct values dropped from 35 (~30% reporting symptoms around the positive test) to 28 (~60% reporting symptoms), below 28 the percentages reporting symptoms increased only slightly (to ~70% at Ct=10) (Figure 2).
evidence: The manuscript describes the relationship between Ct values and symptom reporting and references Figure 2.

claim: 21,329 (77%) positive tests had 'higher' evidence, 4,741 (17%) had 'moderate' evidence, and 1,809 (6%) had 'lower' evidence supporting genuine presence of viral RNA.
source: Combining information on Ct values, symptoms and pre-test probability of being positive, 21,329 (77%), 4741 (17%), and 1809 (6%) positive tests had 'higher', 'moderate', or 'lower' evidence supporting genuine presence of viral RNA (Table 2; definitions in Materials and methods).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific counts and percentages for different evidence levels.

claim: 'Higher' evidence positives were more likely to be symptomatic than 'moderate' evidence positives (p<0.0001).
source: Even though 'higher' evidence was based only on number of genes detected (two or three), 'higher' evidence positives were more likely to be symptomatic than 'moderate' evidence positives (p<0.0001), but were similarly likely to have occupational risk factors (p=0.48).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results comparing symptom rates between evidence levels.

claim: 'Higher' evidence positives were similarly likely to have occupational risk factors as 'moderate' evidence positives (p=0.48).
source: Even though 'higher' evidence was based only on number of genes detected (two or three), 'higher' evidence positives were more likely to be symptomatic than 'moderate' evidence positives (p<0.0001), but were similarly likely to have occupational risk factors (p=0.48).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results comparing occupational risk factors between evidence levels.

claim: 'Higher' evidence positives were more likely to occur in households with other positives (p<0.0001).
source: 'Higher' evidence positives were more likely to occur in households with other positives (p<0.0001).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results showing the relationship between evidence level and household positivity.

claim: Ct values were independently lower (i.e. viral loads higher) with more genes detected (8.2 lower in triple-gene vs single-gene positives [95% CI 7.9–8.5]).
source: In multivariable regression models, Ct values were independently lower (i.e. viral loads higher) with more genes detected (8.2 lower in triple-gene vs single-gene positives [95% CI 7.9–8.5]), if symptoms were reported around the test (2.0 lower [1.8–2.2]), at the first positive identified per participant (2.2 lower than subsequent positives [2.2–2.5]), and if the positive was not the participant's first test in the study (0.6 lower [0.2–0.9]) (all p<0.0001; Supplementary file 2A; see Materials and methods for details of collection of symptoms).
evidence: The manuscript provides multivariable regression results showing the relationship between Ct values and number of genes detected.

claim: Ct values were independently lower if symptoms were reported around the test (2.0 lower [1.8–2.2]).
source: In multivariable regression models, Ct values were independently lower (i.e. viral loads higher) with more genes detected (8.2 lower in triple-gene vs single-gene positives [95% CI 7.9–8.5]), if symptoms were reported around the test (2.0 lower [1.8–2.2]), at the first positive identified per participant (2.2 lower than subsequent positives [2.2–2.5]), and if the positive was not the participant's first test in the study (0.6 lower [0.2–0.9]) (all p<0.0001; Supplementary file 2A; see Materials and methods for details of collection of symptoms).
evidence: The manuscript provides multivariable regression results showing the relationship between Ct values and symptom reporting.

claim: Ct values were independently lower at the first positive identified per participant (2.2 lower than subsequent positives [2.2–2.5]).
source: In multivariable regression models, Ct values were independently lower (i.e. viral loads higher) with more genes detected (8.2 lower in triple-gene vs single-gene positives [95% CI 7.9–8.5]), if symptoms were reported around the test (2.0 lower [1.8–2.2]), at the first positive identified per participant (2.2 lower than subsequent positives [2.2–2.5]), and if the positive was not the participant's first test in the study (0.6 lower [0.2–0.9]) (all p<0.0001; Supplementary file 2A; see Materials and methods for details of collection of symptoms).
evidence: The manuscript provides multivariable regression results showing the relationship between Ct values and whether the positive was the first for the participant.

claim: Ct values were independently lower if the positive was not the participant's first test in the study (0.6 lower [0.2–0.9]).
source: In multivariable regression models, Ct values were independently lower (i.e. viral loads higher) with more genes detected (8.2 lower in triple-gene vs single-gene positives [95% CI 7.9–8.5]), if symptoms were reported around the test (2.0 lower [1.8–2.2]), at the first positive identified per participant (2.2 lower than subsequent positives [2.2–2.5]), and if the positive was not the participant's first test in the study (0.6 lower [0.2–0.9]) (all p<0.0001; Supplementary file 2A; see Materials and methods for details of collection of symptoms).
evidence: The manuscript provides multivariable regression results showing the relationship between Ct values and whether the positive was the participant's first test.

claim: Men had slightly lower Ct values than women (0.3 lower [0.1–0.5] p=0.001).
source: By far the strongest effect was associated with triple-gene positives. Men had slightly lower Ct values than women (0.3 lower [0.1–0.5] p=0.001), and there was marginal evidence of lower values in those reporting non-white ethnicity (0.3 lower [0–0.6] p=0.08).
evidence: The manuscript provides multivariable regression results showing the relationship between Ct values and sex.

claim: There was marginal evidence of lower Ct values in those reporting non-white ethnicity (0.3 lower [0–0.6] p=0.08).
source: By far the strongest effect was associated with triple-gene positives. Men had slightly lower Ct values than women (0.3 lower [0.1–0.5] p=0.001), and there was marginal evidence of lower values in those reporting non-white ethnicity (0.3 lower [0–0.6] p=0.08).
evidence: The manuscript provides multivariable regression results showing the relationship between Ct values and ethnicity.

claim: Ct values were lower in those reporting cough/fever/anosmia/ageusia (2.5 lower [2.3–2.8]) than other symptoms only (0.9 lower [0.7–1.2]).
source: Compared with those not reporting symptoms, Ct values were lower in those reporting cough/fever/anosmia/ageusia (2.5 lower [2.3–2.8]) than other symptoms only (0.9 lower [0.7–1.2]; heterogeneity p<0.0001).
evidence: The manuscript provides multivariable regression results showing the relationship between Ct values and specific symptoms.

claim: After adjusting for multiple factors, there was no evidence of independent effects of age (p=0.33) or deprivation (p=0.67) on Ct values.
source: After adjusting for these factors, there was no evidence of independent effects of age (p=0.33) or deprivation (p=0.67, Supplementary file 2A).
evidence: The manuscript provides multivariable regression results showing no independent effects of age or deprivation.

claim: Ct values were 1.4 (1.2–1.6) lower in individuals where another household member was positive at any point in the study (p<0.0001).
source: Even after adjusting for these factors, Ct values were 1.4 (1.2–1.6) lower in individuals where another household member was positive at any point in the study (p<0.0001; other effects similar).
evidence: The manuscript provides multivariable regression results showing the relationship between Ct values and household positivity.

claim: Excluding number of genes detected and symptoms as potential mediators, Ct values were slightly lower with increasing deprivation (p=0.0005; Ct 1.0 lower in the most vs least deprived [95% CI 0.6–1.5]).
source: However, number of genes detected and symptoms are both potential mediators of effects of demographic factors (Appendix 1—figure 2). Excluding these potential mediators (number of genes detected, symptoms), Ct values remained independently lower (i.e. viral loads higher) at the first positive identified per participant, where the positive was not the participant's first test in the study, and in men, but were also slightly lower with increasing deprivation (p=0.0005; Ct 1.0 lower in the most vs least deprived [95% CI 0.6–1.5]) and in younger adults (p=0.0001; those aged 17–24 1.0 lower [0.3–1.7] than those under 12, and 1.4 lower [0.8–2.0] than those aged 70+) (Supplementary file 2B).
evidence: The manuscript provides multivariable regression results excluding potential mediators showing the relationship between Ct values and deprivation.

claim: Excluding number of genes detected and symptoms as potential mediators, Ct values were slightly lower in younger adults (p=0.0001; those aged 17–24 1.0 lower [0.3–1.7] than those under 12, and 1.4 lower [0.8–2.0] than those aged 70+).
source: However, number of genes detected and symptoms are both potential mediators of effects of demographic factors (Appendix 1—figure 2). Excluding these potential mediators (number of genes detected, symptoms), Ct values remained independently lower (i.e. viral loads higher) at the first positive identified per participant, where the positive was not the participant's first test in the study, and in men, but were also slightly lower with increasing deprivation (p=0.0005; Ct 1.0 lower in the most vs least deprived [95% CI 0.6–1.5]) and in younger adults (p=0.0001; those aged 17–24 1.0 lower [0.3–1.7] than those under 12, and 1.4 lower [0.8–2.0] than those aged 70+) (Supplementary file 2B).
evidence: The manuscript provides multivariable regression results excluding potential mediators showing the relationship between Ct values and age.

claim: There were strong effects of calendar time on the distribution of Ct values (p<0.0001).
source: There were strong effects of calendar time on the distribution of Ct values (Figure 3A,B), the percentages self-reporting symptoms, or cough/fever/anosmia/ageusia (Figure 3C), and strength of evidence supporting each positive result (Figure 3D; all p<0.0001).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results showing temporal variation in Ct values and references Figure 3.

claim: Ct values were markedly higher in July–August 2020 when population positivity rates were low.
source: In particular, Ct values were markedly higher in July–August 2020 when population positivity rates were low, with correspondingly very low percentages with symptoms at/around positive tests, and more 'lower' evidence positives.
evidence: The manuscript describes temporal patterns in Ct values during specific time periods.

claim: Decreases in Ct values in late August/early September and December 2020 coincided with increases in percentages reporting symptoms and of 'higher' evidence positives.
source: Decreases in Ct values in late August/early September and December 2020 coincided with increases in percentages reporting symptoms and of 'higher' evidence positives, and, in England (Figure 3B), with initial rises in official estimates of positivity rates (Office for National Statistics, 2021) after very low rates in July/early August 2020, and with much stronger rises in December 2020 (expansion of B.1.1.7).
evidence: The manuscript describes temporal patterns in Ct values and their relationship to other measures, citing official statistics.

claim: Ct levels rose as positivity peaked during November 2020 and January 2021 lockdowns.
source: Ct levels rose, and correspondingly percentages reporting symptoms and of 'higher' evidence positives declined, as positivity peaked during November 2020 and January 2021 lockdowns.
evidence: The manuscript describes temporal patterns in Ct values during lockdown periods.

claim: Even within 'higher' evidence positives, median Ct varied strongly over time being higher in July/early August 2020 and after November 2020 and January 2021 lockdowns.
source: However, even within 'higher' evidence positives, median Ct varied strongly over time being higher in July/early August 2020 and after November 2020 and January 2021 lockdowns (Figure 4A).
evidence: The manuscript describes temporal patterns in Ct values within 'higher' evidence positives and references Figure 4A.

claim: 'Lower' evidence positives formed a larger percentage of all tests during July/early August 2020, despite overall positivity rates being very low.
source: 'Lower' evidence positives also formed a larger percentage of all tests during July/early August 2020, despite overall positivity rates being very low (e.g. 0.022% in the 3 weeks starting 20 July 2020; Figure 4B).
evidence: The manuscript describes temporal patterns in the percentage of 'lower' evidence positives and references Figure 4B.

claim: From September 2020, the percentage of 'lower' evidence positives increased proportionately with 'moderate' and 'higher' evidence positives.
source: However, interestingly, from September 2020, the percentage of 'lower' evidence positives increased proportionately with 'moderate' and 'higher' evidence positives (Figure 4B).
evidence: The manuscript describes temporal patterns in the percentage of different evidence levels and references Figure 4B.

claim: The lowest non-zero observed rate of 'low evidence' positives was 0.005%, providing an upper bound on the rate of false-positives.
source: The lowest non-zero observed rate of 'low evidence' positives was 0.005% (both in early June and late August), providing an upper bound on the rate of false-positives as defined by identifying virus when none present.
evidence: The manuscript provides a specific rate of 'low evidence' positives and interprets it as an upper bound on false-positives.

claim: Less than 5% of antibody tests taken >30 days before the first positive swab were positive.
source: One or more IgG S-antibody results were available for 6540 (30%) participants with positive swabs. Less than 5% of antibody tests taken >30 days before the first positive swab (not necessarily the onset of infection) were positive (Figure 5), rising to 12% in the 30 days before the first swab positive (likely reflecting late detection of infection), 47% in the following 14 days, and then 72–81% thereafter.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages of antibody positivity at different time points and references Figure 5.

claim: Antibody positivity rose to 12% in the 30 days before the first swab positive.
source: One or more IgG S-antibody results were available for 6540 (30%) participants with positive swabs. Less than 5% of antibody tests taken >30 days before the first positive swab (not necessarily the onset of infection) were positive (Figure 5), rising to 12% in the 30 days before the first swab positive (likely reflecting late detection of infection), 47% in the following 14 days, and then 72–81% thereafter.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages of antibody positivity at different time points and references Figure 5.

claim: Antibody positivity rose to 47% in the 14 days following the first positive swab.
source: One or more IgG S-antibody results were available for 6540 (30%) participants with positive swabs. Less than 5% of antibody tests taken >30 days before the first positive swab (not necessarily the onset of infection) were positive (Figure 5), rising to 12% in the 30 days before the first swab positive (likely reflecting late detection of infection), 47% in the following 14 days, and then 72–81% thereafter.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages of antibody positivity at different time points and references Figure 5.

claim: Antibody positivity was 72–81% more than 14 days after the first positive swab.
source: One or more IgG S-antibody results were available for 6540 (30%) participants with positive swabs. Less than 5% of antibody tests taken >30 days before the first positive swab (not necessarily the onset of infection) were positive (Figure 5), rising to 12% in the 30 days before the first swab positive (likely reflecting late detection of infection), 47% in the following 14 days, and then 72–81% thereafter.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages of antibody positivity at different time points and references Figure 5.

claim: Of 6189 participants with one or more antibody tests after their first positive swab, 4808 (78%) were ever antibody-positive.
source: Overall, of 6189 participants with one or more antibody tests after their first positive swab, 4808 (78%) were ever antibody-positive; with higher rates in those reporting symptoms around their first positive swab (2945/3315 [89%] vs 1863/2874 [65%] of those not reporting symptoms, p<0.0001).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific counts and percentages of antibody positivity after positive swabs.

claim: Antibody positivity rates were higher in those reporting symptoms around their first positive swab (89%) vs those not reporting symptoms (65%).
source: Overall, of 6189 participants with one or more antibody tests after their first positive swab, 4808 (78%) were ever antibody-positive; with higher rates in those reporting symptoms around their first positive swab (2945/3315 [89%] vs 1863/2874 [65%] of those not reporting symptoms, p<0.0001).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages of antibody positivity stratified by symptom status with statistical test results.

claim: Median Ct values were significantly lower in those ever antibody-positive to date (24.9 [18.5–31.0]) vs those not antibody-positive (33.0 [29.9–34.3]).
source: Median (IQR) Ct values were also significantly lower in those ever antibody-positive to date (24.9 [18.5–31.0] vs 33.0 [29.9–34.3] in those not antibody-positive, p<0.0001).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific Ct values stratified by antibody status with statistical test results.

claim: The COVID-19 Infection Survey randomly selects private households to provide a representative UK sample.
source: In brief (details in Materials and methods), the survey randomly selects private households to provide a representative UK sample, recruiting all consenting individuals aged 2 years or older currently resident in each household to provide information on demographics, symptoms, contacts and relevant behaviours and self-taken nose and throat swabs for RT-PCR testing (Pouwels et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript describes the study design and cites a reference for the survey methodology.

claim: The survey recruits all consenting individuals aged 2 years or older currently resident in each household.
source: In brief (details in Materials and methods), the survey randomly selects private households to provide a representative UK sample, recruiting all consenting individuals aged 2 years or older currently resident in each household to provide information on demographics, symptoms, contacts and relevant behaviours and self-taken nose and throat swabs for RT-PCR testing (Pouwels et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript describes the study design and cites a reference for the survey methodology.

claim: RT-PCR for three SARS-CoV-2 genes (N protein, S protein, and ORF1ab) used the Thermo Fisher TaqPath RT-PCR COVID-19 Kit.
source: RT-PCR for three SARS-CoV-2 genes (N protein, S protein, and ORF1ab) used the Thermo Fisher TaqPath RT-PCR COVID-19 Kit, analysed using UgenTec Fast Finder 3.300.5 (TaqMan 2019-nCoV Assay Kit V2 UK NHS ABI 7500 v2.1).
evidence: The manuscript describes the specific RT-PCR methodology used in the study.

claim: Samples are called positive in the presence of at least single N gene and/or ORF1ab but may be accompanied with S gene.
source: Samples are called positive in the presence of at least single N gene and/or ORF1ab but may be accompanied with S gene (one, two, or three gene positives). There is no specific Ct threshold for determining positivity. S gene is not considered a reliable single-gene positive (as of mid-May 2020).
evidence: The manuscript describes the criteria for calling samples positive.

claim: There is no specific Ct threshold for determining positivity in the assay used.
source: Samples are called positive in the presence of at least single N gene and/or ORF1ab but may be accompanied with S gene (one, two, or three gene positives). There is no specific Ct threshold for determining positivity. S gene is not considered a reliable single-gene positive (as of mid-May 2020).
evidence: The manuscript describes the criteria for calling samples positive.

claim: S gene is not considered a reliable single-gene positive (as of mid-May 2020).
source: Samples are called positive in the presence of at least single N gene and/or ORF1ab but may be accompanied with S gene (one, two, or three gene positives). There is no specific Ct threshold for determining positivity. S gene is not considered a reliable single-gene positive (as of mid-May 2020).
evidence: The manuscript describes the criteria for calling samples positive.

claim: Antibody titres were considered positive above 8 million units on the original fluorometric version of the assay.
source: Antibody titres were considered positive above 8 million units (National SARS-CoV-2 Serology Assay Evaluation Group, 2020) on the original fluorometric version of the assay and 42 units on the colorimetric version of the assay (used from 1 March 2021).
evidence: The manuscript describes the antibody assay thresholds and cites a reference for the assay evaluation.

claim: Antibody titres were considered positive above 42 units on the colorimetric version of the assay (used from 1 March 2021).
source: Antibody titres were considered positive above 8 million units (National SARS-CoV-2 Serology Assay Evaluation Group, 2020) on the original fluorometric version of the assay and 42 units on the colorimetric version of the assay (used from 1 March 2021).
evidence: The manuscript describes the antibody assay thresholds and cites a reference for the assay evaluation.

claim: Recruitment started 26 April 2020 in England, 29 June 2020 in Wales, 29 July 2020 in Northern Ireland, and 21 September 2020 in Scotland.
source: Recruitment started 26 April 2020 in England, 29 June 2020 in Wales, 29 July 2020 in Northern Ireland, and 21 September 2020 in Scotland.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific dates for recruitment start in different UK countries.

claim: Ct values were independently associated with several factors, including symptoms at/around the test as previously reported.
source: In this large community surveillance study, we found wide variation in Ct values (a proxy for viral load). Whilst Ct values were independently associated with several factors, including symptoms at/around the test as previously reported (Edwards et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2020), their effects were small compared with population-level variability.
evidence: The manuscript describes findings on Ct value associations and cites previous studies.

claim: The effects of factors associated with Ct values were small compared with population-level variability.
source: In this large community surveillance study, we found wide variation in Ct values (a proxy for viral load). Whilst Ct values were independently associated with several factors, including symptoms at/around the test as previously reported (Edwards et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2020), their effects were small compared with population-level variability.
evidence: The manuscript describes findings on Ct value associations and their relative magnitude.

claim: Triple-gene positives and S-gene target failures compatible with the Alpha/B.1.1.7 variant without reported symptoms had widely varying Ct, including many with low values, potentially explaining variation in dispersion ('k') and super-spreading events.
source: Notably both triple-gene positives and S-gene target failures compatible with the Alpha/B.1.1.7 variant without reported symptoms had widely varying Ct, including many with low values (Figure 3A), potentially explaining variation in dispersion ('k') and super-spreading events, particularly from those without symptoms but with low Ct/high viral loads (Endo et al., 2020; Rasmussen and Popescu, 2021).
evidence: The manuscript describes findings on Ct value variation and speculates on implications for transmission, citing relevant references.

claim: Lower Ct in those reporting cough/fever/anosmia/ageusia than other symptoms supports the importance of the 'classic' symptoms for identifying the most infectious cases.
source: We found lower Ct in those reporting cough/fever/anosmia/ageusia than other symptoms, and other symptoms vs no symptoms, supporting the importance of the 'classic' symptoms for identifying the most infectious cases.
evidence: The manuscript describes findings on Ct values and symptoms and infers implications for case identification.

claim: Lower Ct values in the first positive per participant likely reflects the natural history of viral load post-infection.
source: Lower Ct values in the first positive per participant likely reflects the natural history of viral load post-infection, and higher Ct values in those positive at their first test in the study over-representation of long-term shedders in this group.
evidence: The manuscript describes findings on Ct values and infers biological explanations.

claim: Higher Ct values in those positive at their first test in the study reflects over-representation of long-term shedders in this group.
source: Lower Ct values in the first positive per participant likely reflects the natural history of viral load post-infection, and higher Ct values in those positive at their first test in the study over-representation of long-term shedders in this group.
evidence: The manuscript describes findings on Ct values and infers biological explanations.

claim: Lower Ct values in men and those reporting non-white ethnicity are consistent with poorer outcomes in these groups.
source: Lower Ct values in men and those reporting non-white ethnicity, although small, are consistent with poorer outcomes in these groups.
evidence: The manuscript describes findings on Ct values and relates them to known outcome disparities.

claim: Small effects of age and deprivation on Ct values were mediated by self-reported symptoms and number of positive genes.
source: Interestingly, small effects of age and deprivation were mediated by self-reported symptoms and number of positive genes. That is, when adjusting for these latter factors no association was observed with Ct, but without adjustment younger individuals (as shown in Jones et al., 2020 but not Jacot et al., 2020) and those from more deprived areas had slightly lower Ct values, suggesting that these factors may affect the intrinsic level of virus present (Appendix 1—figure 2).
evidence: The manuscript describes findings on Ct values and mediation analysis, citing relevant references.

claim: Younger individuals and those from more deprived areas had slightly lower Ct values without adjustment for symptoms and number of genes, suggesting that these factors may affect the intrinsic level of virus present.
source: Interestingly, small effects of age and deprivation were mediated by self-reported symptoms and number of positive genes. That is, when adjusting for these latter factors no association was observed with Ct, but without adjustment younger individuals (as shown in Jones et al., 2020 but not Jacot et al., 2020) and those from more deprived areas had slightly lower Ct values, suggesting that these factors may affect the intrinsic level of virus present (Appendix 1—figure 2).
evidence: The manuscript describes findings on Ct values and infers biological implications, citing relevant references.

claim: The findings strongly refute hypotheses that declines in positivity during July/early August 2020 were due to declines in viral fitness.
source: Ct values varied strongly over time, as did symptoms and evidence supporting positives, suggesting changing viral burden in infection cases, with less severe infections during July/early August 2020. This strongly refutes hypotheses that declines in positivity during this period were due to declines in viral fitness.
evidence: The manuscript describes findings on temporal Ct variation and infers implications for viral fitness hypotheses.

claim: Higher Ct values were noted in the English point-prevalence surveillance study, REACT, during July/early August 2020.
source: During this time, higher Ct values were also noted in the English point-prevalence surveillance study, REACT (Riley and Ainslie, 2020b), and lower virus levels in Lausanne, Switzerland (Jacot et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites other studies that observed similar temporal patterns in Ct values.

claim: Lower virus levels were noted in Lausanne, Switzerland during July/early August 2020.
source: During this time, higher Ct values were also noted in the English point-prevalence surveillance study, REACT (Riley and Ainslie, 2020b), and lower virus levels in Lausanne, Switzerland (Jacot et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites other studies that observed similar temporal patterns in viral load.

claim: Ct values were higher even in 'higher' evidence positives during July/early August 2020, consistent with shifting viral burden.
source: However, Ct values were higher even in 'higher' evidence positives during this period, consistent with shifting viral burden (Figure 4A).
evidence: The manuscript describes findings on temporal Ct variation within evidence categories and infers implications.

claim: The shift in viral burden may explain the preceding shift towards 'moderate' evidence positives and the concurrent higher percentage of 'lower' evidence positives.
source: Such a shift may also explain the preceding shift towards 'moderate' evidence positives and the concurrent higher percentage of 'lower' evidence positives, since the less virus present, the less likely it is to be detected on multiple genes.
evidence: The manuscript infers a causal relationship between viral burden and evidence categories.

claim: The findings are consistent with lower viral inoculum during July/early August 2020.
source: Whilst these findings are consistent with lower viral inoculum during this period (Gandhi et al., 2020), we cannot assess whether this is predominantly due to behaviour (e.g. increased time outdoors, face mask use Gandhi and Rutherford, 2020) or other reasons (e.g. environmental/climatic factors, including relating to transport of swabs for testing).
evidence: The manuscript speculates on possible explanations for the findings and cites relevant references.

claim: Decreases in Ct values in July/early August 2020 preceded increases in positivity rates in England.
source: Whilst decreases in Ct values in July/early August 2020 preceded increases in positivity rates in England, later declines in Ct in early December coincided with, rather than preceded, increases in positivity due to B.1.1.7 expansion.
evidence: The manuscript describes temporal relationships between Ct values and positivity rates.

claim: Later declines in Ct in early December coincided with, rather than preceded, increases in positivity due to B.1.1.7 expansion.
source: Whilst decreases in Ct values in July/early August 2020 preceded increases in positivity rates in England, later declines in Ct in early December coincided with, rather than preceded, increases in positivity due to B.1.1.7 expansion.

claim: The coincidence of Ct decline with positivity increase in December may potentially reflect faster transmission of B.1.1.7.
source: This may potentially reflect faster transmission of B.1.1.7 but may also reflect greater sensitivity to changes in Ct distribution when case numbers are small.
evidence: The manuscript speculates on possible explanations for the temporal patterns observed.

claim: Around 70% of positives had two or three genes detected ('higher' evidence), providing assurance in overall results.
source: We used laboratory, clinical, and demographic evidence to classify our confidence in positive results. Around 70% had two or three genes detected ('higher' evidence), providing assurance in overall results, with only 0.1% of Ct values over 37.
evidence: The manuscript describes the classification system and interprets the implications for result confidence.

claim: REACT has validated a Ct threshold of 37 for single-gene positives for their test performed in Germany.
source: Whilst Ct values are not directly comparable between studies, REACT has also validated a Ct threshold of 37 for single-gene positives for their test performed in Germany (Riley and Ainslie, 2020b), and in the Public Health England (PHE) Schools study, only samples with Ct<37 were positive on repeat testing of the same swab at PHE laboratories (Ladhani et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites other studies that have validated similar Ct thresholds.

claim: In the Public Health England (PHE) Schools study, only samples with Ct<37 were positive on repeat testing of the same swab at PHE laboratories.
source: Whilst Ct values are not directly comparable between studies, REACT has also validated a Ct threshold of 37 for single-gene positives for their test performed in Germany (Riley and Ainslie, 2020b), and in the Public Health England (PHE) Schools study, only samples with Ct<37 were positive on repeat testing of the same swab at PHE laboratories (Ladhani et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites other studies that have validated similar Ct thresholds.

claim: The false-positive rate would generally be expected to be approximately constant over time, since it is either random or driven by external factors.
source: However, every diagnostic test has false-positives, here defining a false-positive as detection of virus by RT-PCR when no virus is present in a sample, so some of our single-gene 'lower', or even 'moderate', evidence positives are inevitably false. However, the false-positive rate (as defined) would generally be expected to be approximately constant over time, since it is either random or driven by external factors, although cross-contamination (which should be minimised by good laboratory practice) may theoretically be related to background prevalence/viral load.
evidence: The manuscript applies general knowledge about diagnostic test characteristics to interpret findings.

claim: Variation in the percentage of all tests accounted for by 'lower' evidence positives supports more genuinely lower-level infections occurring during the summer.
source: Variation in the percentage of all tests accounted for by 'lower' evidence positives, and in particular the proportionate increases in 'lower' evidence positives as 'higher' evidence positives increased during September 2020 supports more genuinely lower-level infections occurring during the summer, and an overall false-positive rate for this test of below ~0.005% that is at least 99.995% specificity.
evidence: The manuscript infers the presence of genuine lower-level infections from temporal patterns in evidence categories.

claim: The overall false-positive rate for this test is below ~0.005%, corresponding to at least 99.995% specificity.
source: Variation in the percentage of all tests accounted for by 'lower' evidence positives, and in particular the proportionate increases in 'lower' evidence positives as 'higher' evidence positives increased during September 2020 supports more genuinely lower-level infections occurring during the summer, and an overall false-positive rate for this test of below ~0.005% that is at least 99.995% specificity.
evidence: The manuscript infers the false-positive rate from temporal patterns in evidence categories.

claim: A strong relationship between Ct values and infection in contacts is observed.
source: First, it is clear that the detection of viral RNA is neither the same as infectiousness, although a strong relationship between Ct values and infection in contacts is observed (Lee et al., 2021), nor a 'disease' in its own right.
evidence: The manuscript cites a study showing the relationship between Ct values and transmission.

claim: Infectious virus was recovered from only 8% (95% CI 3–18%) of samples with Ct>35 in a PHE study.
source: Although they were a small minority (6%), one question is whether single-gene positives with high Ct (defined as ≥34 in our study) solely represent long-term shedding of non-transmissible virus (Moraz et al., 2020), with, for example, infectious virus recovered from only 8% (95% CI 3–18%) of samples with Ct>35 in a PHE study (Singanayagam et al., 2020) and studies reporting no growth of virus for Ct thresholds from >24 to >34 or higher (Jefferson et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies on the relationship between Ct values and viral culture.

claim: Studies report no growth of virus for Ct thresholds from >24 to >34 or higher.
source: Although they were a small minority (6%), one question is whether single-gene positives with high Ct (defined as ≥34 in our study) solely represent long-term shedding of non-transmissible virus (Moraz et al., 2020), with, for example, infectious virus recovered from only 8% (95% CI 3–18%) of samples with Ct>35 in a PHE study (Singanayagam et al., 2020) and studies reporting no growth of virus for Ct thresholds from >24 to >34 or higher (Jefferson et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies on the relationship between Ct values and viral culture.

claim: Ct values were 0.6 higher in positives that were a participant's first study test, where long-term shedders would be expected to be overrepresented.
source: Ct values were 0.6 higher in positives that were a participant's first study test (where long-term shedders would be expected to be overrepresented), but these formed only 14% of the positives.
evidence: The manuscript describes findings on Ct values and infers implications for long-term shedding.

claim: A recent systematic review estimated that 95% of adults with laboratory confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection developed IgG antibodies, peaking around 25 days.
source: A recent systematic review estimated that 95% of adults with laboratory confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection developed IgG antibodies (Arkhipova-Jenkins et al., 2021), peaking around 25 days.
evidence: The manuscript cites a systematic review on seroconversion rates.

claim: Only 23% of studies in the systematic review were in outpatient settings and 14% included only participants with asymptomatic or mild disease.
source: However, only 23% of included studies were in outpatient settings and 14% included only participants with asymptomatic or mild disease.
evidence: The manuscript describes characteristics of studies included in the cited systematic review.

claim: The community setting, with higher percentages not reporting symptoms and higher Ct values, likely explains the lower overall seroconversion estimate compared with previous studies.
source: Our community setting, with higher percentages not reporting symptoms and higher Ct values (both associated with not seroconverting), likely explains our lower overall seroconversion estimate compared with these previous studies.
evidence: The manuscript infers reasons for differences between their findings and previous studies.

claim: Presumed re-infections have been reported elsewhere, including in individuals without previous functional and/or durable antibody responses.
source: We observed a small number of new swab positives in antibody-positive individuals: unfortunately whole-genome sequence data were not available to confirm potential re-infections. Presumed re-infections have been reported elsewhere (Tomassini et al., 2021), including in individuals without previous functional and/or durable antibody responses (Goldman et al., 2020; To et al., 2020), and may remain relevant to virus transmission, whether they occur with or without symptoms.
evidence: The manuscript cites other studies that have reported re-infections.

claim: Re-infections may occur in the presence of anti-spike antibodies, which correlate with neutralising antibody titres.
source: Our data and others (Lumley et al., 2021) suggest that these may occur in the presence of anti-spike antibodies, which correlate with neutralising antibody titres.
evidence: The manuscript describes findings on re-infections and cites supporting studies.

claim: Estimates of asymptomatic infection rates vary, being 17–41% overall in recent reviews.
source: Estimates of asymptomatic infection rates vary, being 17–41% overall in recent reviews (Buitrago-Garcia et al., 2020; Byambasuren et al., 2020), but these included many studies of contacts of confirmed cases.
evidence: The manuscript cites reviews on asymptomatic infection rates.

claim: Higher prevalence of asymptomatic infection has been reported in screening of defined populations (30%).
source: Higher prevalence of asymptomatic infection has been reported in screening of defined populations (30% [Buitrago-Garcia et al., 2020]) and community surveillance (e.g. 42% Lavezzo et al., 2020, 72% Riley and Ainslie, 2020a).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies on asymptomatic infection prevalence in different settings.

claim: Studies have generally indicated lower rates of transmission from asymptomatic infection.
source: Studies have generally indicated lower rates of transmission from asymptomatic infection (Buitrago-Garcia et al., 2020; Byambasuren et al., 2020), this may be a proxy for SARS-CoV-2 viral load as a key determinant of transmission.
evidence: The manuscript cites studies on transmission from asymptomatic infection and infers a relationship with viral load.

claim: The findings support the use of Ct values and genes detected more broadly in public testing programmes as an 'early warning' system for shifts in potential infectious load and transmission.
source: Our findings support the use of Ct values and genes detected more broadly in public testing programmes, predominantly testing symptomatic individuals and case contacts, as an 'early warning' system for shifts in potential infectious load and hence transmission, and hence the risks posed by individuals to others.
evidence: The manuscript infers implications of the findings for public health practice.

claim: Theoretical work has proposed linking effective reproduction numbers to population-level Ct.
source: This has recently also been proposed on the basis of theoretical work linking effective reproduction numbers to population-level Ct (Hay et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites theoretical work supporting the use of Ct values for surveillance.

claim: Declines in mean and median Ct values preceded or at least coincided with increases in office estimates of positivity rates.
source: In our study, declines in mean and median Ct values preceded or at least coincided with increases in office estimates of positivity rates (Figure 3B); given the far larger numbers that would be available in testing programmes, future research should investigate whether the greater power afforded by continuous outcomes could lead to significantly earlier detection of future positivity increases, particularly within small geographical areas.
evidence: The manuscript describes temporal relationships between Ct values and positivity rates and speculates on future applications.

claim: Ct data are widely available within-laboratory management systems.
source: Ct data are widely available within-laboratory management systems; providing comparisons across the wide variety of commercial assays were interpreted carefully, they could be used alongside available risk factor and symptom information to facilitate more informed and effective individual-level and public health responses to the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic.
evidence: The manuscript applies general knowledge about laboratory systems and speculates on potential applications.

claim: With 0.1% true prevalence, testing 100,000 individuals with a 99.9% specific test with perfect sensitivity gives 100 true-positives and 100 false-positives (PPV 50%).
source: For example, with 0.1% true prevalence, testing 100,000 individuals with a 99.9% specific test with perfect sensitivity gives 100 true-positives, but also 100 false-positives (positive predictive value [PPV] 50%), whereas specificity of 99.5% increases false-positives to 500 (PPV = 17%), and of 99.0% to 999 (PPV = 9%), with even lower PPV with imperfect sensitivity (Adams et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript provides calculations based on test characteristics and cites a reference.

claim: Infection without recognition has the potential for onward transmission.
source: Ultimately, the importance of asymptomatic and low virus-level infections depends on their transmissibility and their prevalence; regardless of limitations in symptom ascertainment, infection without recognition has the potential for onward transmission and unascertained infections are likely critical for avoiding resurgence after lifting lockdown (Hao et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript applies general knowledge about transmission and cites a supporting reference.
